AC9M1N01.title: Compare the whole number
AC9M1N01.goal: Connect a numeral to its groups and position, including numbers past 100.
steps: Build 97 with 9 tens and 7 ones. Build 103 with 1 hundred, no tens and 3 ones.
One hundred is already more than 97. Comparing only the final digits would miss the hundred.
On a number line, 97 comes before 100 and 103 comes after it. So 103 is greater.
AC9M1N01.mistake: Looking at the ones digit first can give the wrong comparison. Compare the complete quantities; start with the largest place.
checks: Order 89, 108 and 98 from least to greatest.
Build or sketch the tens and hundreds first.
89, 98, 108. The two numbers below 100 come first; 8 tens is less than 9 tens.
A number line shows 109, 110, __, 112. What is missing?
Each step adds one.
111. One more than 110 is 111.
homework: Draw bundles and ones to show 114. Label the groups.
One hundred, one ten and four ones; or eleven tens and four ones.
Sam says 92 is greater than 102 because 9 is greater than 1. Explain the mistake.
The digits name different places: 9 tens is 90, while 1 hundred is 100. Therefore 102 is greater.

AC9M1N02.title: Different parts, the same whole
AC9M1N02.goal: Partition a number in more than one way and check that its total stays the same.
AC9M1N02.model: Can 46 be shown as 3 tens and 16 ones?
steps: Start with 4 bundles of ten and 6 singles: 40 and 6 make 46.
Open one bundle. There are now 3 bundles and 16 singles.
The objects have only been regrouped. 30 and 16 still make 46.
AC9M1N02.mistake: Regrouping does not add or remove objects. Count the value of each bundle as ten, not one.
checks: Complete: 35 is 2 tens and __ ones.
Open one of the 3 tens in 35.
Which shows 28: 2 tens and 8 ones, or 1 ten and 8 ones? Explain.
Find the total in each representation.
2 tens and 8 ones. The other representation shows 18.
homework: Show 19 as two parts in two different ways.
For example, 10 + 9 and 12 + 7. Both pairs make 19.
Draw 32 as 3 tens and 2 ones. Regroup one ten and label the new parts.
2 tens and 12 ones. The total remains 32.

AC9M1N03.title: Count groups without losing the leftovers
AC9M1N03.goal: Organise a collection into equal groups, then include any objects left over.
AC9M1N03.model: A collection has 7 full groups of ten and 4 loose counters. How many counters are there?
steps: Count the full groups: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70.
Count on the four loose counters: 71, 72, 73, 74.
There are 74 counters. Grouping makes the count easier to check.
AC9M1N03.mistake: Seven groups of ten contain 70 objects, not 7. Remember to include the loose objects after counting the groups.
checks: There are 11 groups of ten and 6 loose blocks. How many blocks?
Count the tens to 110, then the ones.
116 blocks.
A student counts 6 groups of five as 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. What was missed?
Match one number word to each full group.
The sixth group was missed. The total is 30.
homework: Draw 24 dots organised in groups of two. Write the count underneath.
Show 43 counters using groups of ten and leftovers. Why is this easier to check than scattered dots?
Four groups of ten and three ones. Each full group can be counted as ten, and the three leftovers are visible.

AC9M1N04.title: Use ten as a stepping stone
AC9M1N04.goal: Explain an addition or subtraction strategy using parts within 20.
AC9M1N04.model: Work out 8 + 5 without counting all thirteen objects from one.
steps: Eight needs two more to make ten. Split the five into two and three.
Add the two to eight: 8 + 2 = 10. Three of the five are still left.
10 + 3 = 13, so 8 + 5 = 13. Check by removing five from thirteen.
AC9M1N04.mistake: Do not use the whole five again after making ten. The two used and the three left must still total five.
checks: Use ten to solve 9 + 4. Show how you split 4.
Nine needs one more.
Split 4 into 1 and 3: 9 + 1 + 3 = 13.
Find 14 - 6 by going back through ten.
First remove enough to reach ten.
14 - 4 = 10; two more must be removed, so 10 - 2 = 8.
homework: Use the double 6 + 6 to find 6 + 7. Explain.
6 + 6 = 12. Seven is one more than six, so the total is 13.
Write one addition fact that helps you check 15 - 7 = 8.

AC9M1N05.title: Choose an operation from the situation
AC9M1N05.goal: Represent an additive problem, solve it and say what the answer means.
AC9M1N05.model: A game needs 15 counters. There are 9 on the table. How many more are needed?
steps: Draw a bar for the total of 15. Mark the 9 already there and leave the missing part blank.
Count on from 9 to 15: one to reach 10, then five more. That is six altogether.
Six more counters are needed. Check: 9 + 6 = 15.
AC9M1N05.mistake: The words ‘more’ do not always mean add the two numbers given. Ask what is known and which part is missing.
checks: A book costs $7. You pay with $10. How much change should you receive?
Find the missing part between 7 and 10.
$3. The $7 cost and $3 change together equal the $10 paid.
There are 8 red blocks and 5 blue blocks. Draw a model and find the total.
Both coloured groups are parts of one total.
homework: You have 12 stickers and give away 4. Draw what changes and label what remains.
8 stickers remain; 12 - 4 = 8.
A toy costs $6. You have $4. Do you have enough? Explain how much more is needed.
No. Another $2 is needed because 4 + 2 = 6.

AC9M1N06.title: Sharing and grouping ask different questions
AC9M1N06.goal: Use objects to show whether the unknown is the group size or the number of groups.
AC9M1N06.model: Twelve counters are shared equally onto three mats. How many go on each mat?
steps: Draw three mats because the number of groups is known.
Deal the twelve counters one at a time around the mats until none remain.
Each mat has four. Check that all three groups are equal and that 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
AC9M1N06.mistake: For ‘three mats’, make three groups first. For ‘three in each group’, place three objects together repeatedly instead.
checks: Put 12 counters into groups of 3. How many groups can you make?
Here the size of each group is known.
4 groups, with 3 counters in each.
Ten counters are shared onto two mats as 6 and 4. Is the sharing equal? Repair it.
Move a counter without changing the total.
It is unequal. Move one counter from the group of 6 to the group of 4 to make 5 and 5.
homework: Draw 8 objects shared equally between 4 plates. Label how many are on each.
2 on each plate; four equal groups of two make eight.
Draw 8 objects with 4 on each plate. How many plates are needed?
2 plates. The group size is four and there are two groups.

AC9M1A01.title: Connect a growing picture to its number pattern
AC9M1A01.goal: Recognise, continue and create sequences formed by adding equal groups.
AC9M1A01.model: Each new stage adds one pair of blocks. The first three stages contain 2, 4 and 6 blocks. What comes next?
steps: Build each stage separately: one pair, two pairs, then three pairs.
The number of blocks increases by two each time. Add another pair to make the next stage.
The next stage has 8 blocks. Record the sequence as 2, 4, 6, 8 and explain the same change in the pictures and numbers.
AC9M1A01.mistake: A picture of the same pair repeated three times is not three growing stages. Separate the stages and show the total increasing in each one.
checks: Each row of a table is a new stage. Complete the totals: 5, 10, __, 20. Describe the change.
Compare neighbouring totals and keep that change.
15. Each stage adds five.
A child writes 10, 20, 30, 35 when counting in tens. Correct the last number and explain.
Compare the last jump with the earlier jumps.
40. The last jump should add ten, not five.
homework: Draw four stages of a pattern that starts with 5 dots and adds 5 dots each time. Label each total.
Stages contain 5, 10, 15 and 20 dots; each new stage adds five.
There are four 10-cent coins. Count their value as each coin is added.
10c, 20c, 30c, 40c. The total is 40 cents.

AC9M1A02.title: Find the smallest unit that repeats
AC9M1A02.goal: Identify a repeating unit and use it to continue or create a pattern.
AC9M1A02.model: The pattern is clap, clap, tap, clap, clap, tap. What repeats?
steps: Look for a block of actions that starts again in the same order.
The smallest repeating block is clap, clap, tap. It appears twice.
The next three actions are clap, clap, tap. Change the actions to circle, circle, square to keep the same pattern structure.
AC9M1A02.mistake: Naming only the last action does not identify the unit. Include every part before the pattern starts again.
checks: Continue: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, __, __, __.
Find the three-part unit.
red, blue, blue.
Is 2, 4, 6, 8 a repeating pattern with a repeating unit shown? Explain.
Does the same block restart, or do the numbers grow?
It grows by two. No repeating block of these numbers has restarted.
homework: Create a repeating pattern using two different shapes. Show the unit three times and circle one unit.
For example, circle-square, circle-square, circle-square, with one circle-square unit circled.
A pattern is star, star, moon, star, moon, moon. It should repeat star, star, moon. Which item needs changing?
The fifth item should be a star. The two units then match.

AC9M1M01.title: Compare the same attribute fairly
AC9M1M01.goal: Compare and order objects using a named attribute and evidence.
AC9M1M01.model: Two shelves cannot be moved together. How could you find which is longer?
steps: Use a strip of paper to mark the length of the first shelf, starting at one end.
Place that same strip along the second shelf, lining up the starting ends.
Compare the far ends. The shelf reaching farther is longer. The strip transfers a length between objects.
AC9M1M01.mistake: An object can be taller yet hold less, or larger yet lighter. Decide whether you are comparing length, mass, capacity or duration.
checks: A balance tilts down on the side with the stone. Which is heavier: the stone or the pine cone on the other side?
The heavier side moves down.
The stone is heavier.
Cup A fills 3 identical small scoops; cup B fills 5. Which has greater capacity?
Compare how much each holds using the same scoop.
Cup B. It holds more of the same-sized scoops.
homework: Line up three pencils at one end. Draw them in order from shortest to longest.
Accept an ordering supported by aligned starts and the positions of the other ends.
Two songs start together. Song A finishes first. Which song has the longer duration?
Song B lasts longer because it finishes later after the same start.

AC9M1M02.title: A measurement needs equal units
AC9M1M02.goal: Measure length with equal informal units placed end-to-end.
AC9M1M02.model: A strip is covered exactly by 6 equal cubes in a straight row. How long is it?
steps: Line up the first cube with one end of the strip.
Check that every cube is the same size and touches the next without a gap or overlap.
Count six cubes, so the strip is six cubes long. Name the unit with the number.
AC9M1M02.mistake: Six large units and six small units do not show the same length. Counts can be compared directly only when the units match.
checks: A child leaves spaces between five cubes while measuring a pencil. What must be fixed?
Check the joins between the units.
Move equal cubes end-to-end without gaps, align the start, and measure again.
The same ribbon measures 8 small blocks or 4 longer blocks. Must one measurement be wrong?
Consider the size of the units.
No. Longer units need fewer repetitions to cover the same length.
homework: Measure the long edge of a book using identical paper clips. Draw their end-to-end arrangement and state the unit.
Accept a consistent count with identical units, aligned starts and no gaps or overlaps; describe any leftover part.
Which is longer: a 7-cube strip or a 9-cube strip, using identical cubes? Explain.
The 9-cube strip. It contains two more of the same length unit.

AC9M1M03.title: Choose a useful time unit
AC9M1M03.goal: Describe how long events last and place them in a sensible sequence.
AC9M1M03.model: Would you describe a school lesson in hours or years?
steps: A lesson is part of one school day. A year contains many months and days.
Hours are a useful unit for an event taking part of a day.
Choose units that fit the duration: hours for a lesson, days for a short holiday, months for a long project, and years for a child's age.
AC9M1M03.mistake: The number alone does not tell the duration. Two hours and two months are very different lengths of time.
checks: Today is Tuesday. A game is two days later. On which day is it?
Move forward one day at a time.
Thursday: Wednesday is one day later and Thursday is two days later.
Put one day, one year and one week in order from shortest to longest.
Think about which units fit inside the others.
One day, one week, one year.
homework: A club meets every Friday. Explain why there is one week between two Friday meetings.
The days repeat in a seven-day cycle, so the next Friday is one week later.
Which is a more useful unit for a tree growing from a seedling into a large tree: hours or years? Explain.
Years, because this growth takes a long time, much longer than a few hours.

AC9M1SP01.title: A turned shape keeps its features
AC9M1SP01.goal: Classify shapes by their features rather than size, colour or orientation.
AC9M1SP01.model: A square card is turned so that one corner points upward. Is it still a square?
steps: Trace the boundary and count four straight sides.
Compare the sides and corners: the sides remain equal and the corners still fit a square corner.
Turning the card changes its position, not its features. It remains a square.
AC9M1SP01.mistake: A shape's name does not change just because it is turned or coloured differently. Use its sides and corners as evidence.
checks: A closed flat shape has three straight sides. What shape is it?
Count the sides all the way round.
A triangle.
How are a circle and a triangle different? Give a feature of each.
Compare their boundaries and corners.
A circle has a curved boundary and no corners. A triangle has three straight sides and three corners.
homework: Draw two triangles that look different. Explain why both are triangles.
Accept two closed shapes, each with three straight sides; they may differ in size or side lengths.
Find a rectangular face on an object at home. Draw the face and describe its sides.
For example, a book cover; four straight sides, with opposite sides equal and four square corners.

AC9M1SP02.title: Directions depend on the starting view
AC9M1SP02.goal: Give and follow a sequence of directions with a clear start and facing direction.
AC9M1SP02.model: A robot faces the classroom door. It must move forward two steps, turn right, then move one step.
steps: Mark the starting position and point to the way the robot faces.
Move two steps forward, then turn on the spot to the robot's right.
Move one step in the new facing direction. Check each instruction in its given order.
AC9M1SP02.mistake: Turning right changes where you face; it is not automatically a step sideways. Left and right belong to the person following the directions.
checks: Two children face each other. Will their right hands point to the same side of the room? Explain.
Imagine standing in each child's position.
No. Their facing directions are opposite, so their right sides point to opposite sides of the room.
Why is ‘go forward’ unclear when the starting direction is not given?
Forward is relative to where someone faces.
Different facing directions lead to different routes.
homework: Place a toy at a marked start. Give three instructions to move it around a book and check the route with a partner.
Accept ordered directions that state the initial facing direction and lead to the intended place.
A toy must turn left before moving two steps. What could change if the instructions are followed in reverse order?
It moves two steps in its old direction before turning, so it can finish in a different place.

AC9M1ST01.title: Record each response once
AC9M1ST01.goal: Collect categorical data with clear choices and a reliable record.
AC9M1ST01.model: Five children choose a game: tag, hide-and-seek, tag, ball game, tag. Make a tally record.
steps: Make one row for each game category.
Read each child's choice once and add one tally to its row.
The counts are tag 3, hide-and-seek 1 and ball game 1. The total is five, matching the number of children.
AC9M1ST01.mistake: A child who likes two games must still give one response if the question asks for a single favourite. Make that rule clear before collecting data.
checks: Four answers are apple, pear, pear, apple. Record the count for each category.
Make one mark for each answer.
Apple 2 and pear 2; four responses altogether.
Six students each choose one colour, but the tallies total seven. What should be checked?
Compare the record with the original responses.
Check for a response counted twice or an extra mark. The counts should total six.
homework: Ask three people to choose one favourite from drawing, reading and building. Record every answer in a list or table.
Accept three recorded responses in the stated categories, with one response per person.
Why should everyone answer the same survey question?
The responses then describe the same thing and can be compared fairly.

AC9M1ST02.title: Read a one-to-one display
AC9M1ST02.goal: Use one symbol for each response and compare category frequencies.
AC9M1ST02.model: A picture display shows four circles for walking to school and two circles for cycling. Each circle represents one child.
steps: Read the key: one circle means one child.
Count four walkers and two cyclists. Line up the first two circles in each row to compare.
There are two more walkers than cyclists, and six children altogether.
AC9M1ST02.mistake: Bigger pictures do not represent more children. In a one-to-one display, count the symbols and keep them the same size.
checks: A display shows 3 square symbols for cats and 5 for dogs. One square means one pet. How many more dogs than cats?
Match three symbols from each group.
2 more dogs.
Two categories each have four symbols. What can you conclude?
Compare the counts, not the labels.
Both categories have the same frequency: four each.
homework: Draw a one-to-one display for red 2, green 4 and blue 1. Include a key.
Three labelled rows with 2, 4 and 1 equal-sized symbols; key: one symbol represents one response.
Using that display, state the most common choice and the total number of responses.
Green is most common, with 4 responses. The total is 2 + 4 + 1 = 7.

AC9S1U01.title: Connect a living thing's need to its place
AC9S1U01.goal: Explain how a habitat provides basic needs rather than just naming an animal's home.
AC9S1U01.model: How can a garden meet a bird's needs?
steps: Identify the bird's needs: air, water, food and shelter.
Connect each need to something in the place: air to breathe, water to drink, suitable insects or seeds to eat, and plants that provide cover.
Explain the connection: a leafy shrub can provide shelter; a concrete path by itself does not provide every need.
AC9S1U01.mistake: Plants do not eat soil. Green plants use light to make their food and also need water and air; many get support and nutrients from soil.
checks: A pet has food and shelter but no drinking water. Is every basic need met?
Check each need separately.
No. The pet also needs water.
Why might a leafy plant struggle in a dark cupboard even if it is watered?
Think about what leaves use to make food.
It lacks light needed for healthy growth and food-making.
homework: Observe a plant without damaging it. Name two things its place provides that help it live.
For example, light reaching leaves and water available to roots; air is also acceptable.
A frog's pond dries up. Name one need that becomes harder to meet and explain.
Water becomes harder to obtain; the wet habitat also supports the frog's life. Accept another accurate need-to-place connection.

AC9S1U02.title: Separate today's weather from a seasonal pattern
AC9S1U02.goal: Describe environmental changes and connect them to everyday choices.
AC9S1U02.model: Yesterday was rainy and today is sunny. Does that alone show that the season has changed?
steps: Describe what was observed on each day without guessing a whole season.
Daily weather can change within the same season. Seasonal patterns are noticed over a longer time.
Use today's observations to choose suitable clothing or an activity, and compare many days to discuss a seasonal pattern.
AC9S1U02.mistake: One hot day is not enough to establish a seasonal change. Seasonal patterns also differ between places.
checks: Rain is falling before a walk. Name one sensible change to the plan and why.
Connect the change to the observed weather.
For example, wear a raincoat or use a sheltered route to stay dry.
Which takes longer to observe: clouds moving this afternoon or a tree losing leaves over several weeks?
Compare the times stated.
The tree's change over several weeks.
homework: Observe the sky safely from the ground on two days. Record a similarity and a difference; never look directly at the Sun.
Accept observations such as cloud cover, rain or wind, with the two days identified.
Why might people choose different outdoor activities at different times of year?
Patterns in temperature, rainfall and daylight can make different activities suitable; local conditions vary.

AC9S1U03.title: Change one feature of a push
AC9S1U03.goal: Describe pushes and pulls by strength and direction, then predict an effect.
AC9S1U03.model: The same toy car starts at rest on the same smooth floor. Compare a gentle forward push with a stronger forward push.
steps: Name what stays the same: car, floor, starting place and forward direction.
Name what changes: the strength of the push.
Predict that the stronger push can make the car start moving faster. Test gently with clear space and observe what actually happens.
AC9S1U03.mistake: A push does not always speed an object up. A push opposite its motion can slow it, and a sideways push can change its direction.
checks: You press a soft sponge between your hands. What changes: its shape or only its colour?
Describe what you can observe.
Its shape changes because the pushes compress it.
A rolling ball is gently pushed from the side. What might change?
Consider the direction of the new push.
The ball's direction may change.
homework: Name one safe action that uses a pull and describe its direction.
For example, pulling a drawer towards you to open it.
Predict what happens when a rolling toy car is gently pushed against its direction of travel. Explain.
It can slow or stop because the push acts against its motion.

AC9S1H01.title: Use a pattern to make a useful prediction
AC9S1H01.goal: Connect an observed pattern to an everyday decision and check the result.
AC9S1H01.model: A gardener notices that a pot's soil is often dry after warm, windy days. How could this observation help?
steps: Name the repeated observation: the soil often becomes dry after those conditions.
Predict that the soil may be dry after another warm, windy day.
Check the soil before deciding whether to water. A prediction helps a decision but still needs checking.
AC9S1H01.mistake: A pattern supports a prediction; it does not guarantee that every future event will be identical.
checks: A family sees that washing usually dries faster in moving air. How could they use this pattern?
Choose an action connected to the observation.
Place washing where air can move around it, then check whether it dries.
Why should the gardener check the soil rather than water only because the day was warm?
Other conditions may also affect the soil.
The soil might still be wet, for example after rain or recent watering.
homework: Describe one way someone at home uses an observation to make a decision.
Accept a clear connection, such as noticing dark clouds and checking the forecast before hanging washing outside.
A prediction does not match the result. What should the person do next?
Observe and record the result, then use it to improve the next prediction.

AC9S1I01.title: Turn noticing into an investigable question
AC9S1I01.goal: Ask a question about an observed pattern and give a reason for a prediction.
AC9S1I01.model: You notice the same toy car rolls differently on a rug and on a smooth board. What could you ask?
steps: Describe what you noticed before proposing a reason.
Ask: ‘Will this car roll farther on the rug or on the smooth board when released the same way?’
Predict an outcome using experience: ‘I think it will roll farther on the board because it moved more easily there before.’ The investigation will check the prediction.
AC9S1I01.mistake: A prediction is made before the test and includes a reason. An observation reports what actually happens.
checks: Which can be investigated by observation: ‘Which surface lets this car roll farther?’ or ‘Which car is the nicest?’
Look for a result that can be compared.
The surface question. ‘Nicest’ is a preference unless a clear criterion is agreed.
Complete a prediction: I think the car will roll farther on __ because __.
Use something you have observed or experienced.
Accept a stated surface with a relevant experience-based reason; the prediction need not later be correct.
homework: Notice two objects that roll differently. Write or say one question you could investigate safely.
For example, ‘Will the cylinder or ball roll farther down the same low ramp?’
Why should you keep your original prediction after seeing a different result?
It lets you compare what you expected with what was observed.

AC9S1I02.title: A useful investigation begins with safe steps
AC9S1I02.goal: Suggest and follow a safe sequence to test a prediction.
AC9S1I02.model: A class will compare how a toy car rolls on two surfaces. What should they do before releasing it?
steps: Use a low, stable ramp and check with the teacher that the space is safe.
Clear the path and keep fingers, feet and faces away from the moving car.
Agree on the starting point and release the car without an extra shove. Repeat the agreed procedure on the other surface.
AC9S1I02.mistake: A safety rule should match the actual investigation. ‘Be careful’ is less useful than naming the action that prevents a problem.
checks: Why should a low ramp be secured before a toy car is released?
Think about what might move unexpectedly.
So the ramp does not slip or collapse during the test.
A student wants to test a rolling object near a stairway. What safer location could be used?
Choose a clear, level area with boundaries.
A clear floor area away from stairs, roads and other people, with teacher supervision.
homework: Write three safe steps for comparing how two paper shapes fall from the same low height indoors, with an adult.
For example, clear the space; hold each paper at the same low height without climbing; release and observe one at a time.
Why should everyone follow the agreed steps?
The procedure helps keep people safe and makes the results easier to compare.

AC9S1I03.title: Record what you observe, including the unit
AC9S1I03.goal: Make and record observations and informal measurements accurately.
AC9S1I03.model: A toy car rolls a distance of 7 equal blocks. How should this be recorded?
steps: Place equal blocks end-to-end along the distance from the marked start to the car's stopping place.
Count seven blocks and record ‘7 blocks’, not just ‘7’.
Add a labelled drawing or table entry so another person can understand what was measured.
AC9S1I03.mistake: ‘It went far’ is hard to compare with another result. A recorded distance with the same unit gives clearer evidence.
checks: One result says 5 hand spans and another says 5 paper clips. Are the distances necessarily equal?
Compare the units, not only the number.
No. The units have different lengths.
A leaf has three brown spots. Is ‘three brown spots’ an observation or a prediction?
Was it seen, or expected before looking?
An observation, because it describes what was seen.
homework: Observe a fallen leaf. Draw it and label two visible features without guessing what caused them.
Accept observable features such as colour, number of spots, edge shape or holes.
Measure a small safe object's length using equal blocks and record the number with the unit.
Accept a labelled measurement using equal units placed end-to-end; describe any leftover part.

AC9S1I04.title: Organise observations so a pattern is visible
AC9S1I04.goal: Sort or order information and represent a simple pattern.
AC9S1I04.model: A car travels 4 blocks on a rug and 9 blocks on a board, using the same blocks to measure. Organise the results.
steps: Make a table with headings ‘surface’ and ‘distance in blocks’.
Put 4 beside rug and 9 beside board. Match every result to the correct surface.
Draw one symbol for each block travelled, or compare the table entries. In these trials, the car travelled farther on the board.
AC9S1I04.mistake: Do not change a result to make a tidier pattern. Labels must show which observation each number describes.
checks: Order plant heights of 3, 7 and 5 equal blocks from shortest to tallest.
Compare the counts using the same unit.
3 blocks, 5 blocks, 7 blocks.
Why does a results table need headings?
Imagine reading the numbers without labels.
Headings explain what each number or category represents.
homework: Sort six drawn leaves into smooth-edge and toothed-edge groups. State the sorting rule.
Accept grouping based consistently on the visible edge, with each leaf placed once.
Represent these observations with one symbol per bird: Monday 2 birds, Tuesday 4 birds. Label the days.
Two symbols for Monday, four for Tuesday, with a one-symbol-per-bird key.

AC9S1I05.title: Compare the prediction, the evidence and the test
AC9S1I05.goal: Compare results with predictions and notice whether an investigation was fair.
AC9S1I05.model: You predict a car will roll farther on the board. It travels 8 equal blocks on the board and 5 on the rug, from the same low ramp and release point.
steps: Compare the two recorded distances: eight is farther than five.
State that this result matches the prediction for these trials.
Check what stayed the same and ask whether repeating the test gives a similar result. The surface was the intended change.
AC9S1I05.mistake: If different cars are being compared, the car is the thing that changes. Keep the other relevant conditions alike; do not claim the same object must always be used.
checks: Two groups get slightly different distances using the same procedure. Should one erase its result?
Keep the evidence and look for possible reasons.
No. Compare the observations, check the procedure and repeat if useful.
One car is pushed hard and another is gently released. Is that a fair way to compare the cars? Explain.
More than the car has changed.
No. The starting push also changed. Release them in the same agreed way.
homework: Write a prediction and a different possible observation for a safe rolling test. How would you report the difference?
For example: ‘I predicted the ball would go farther, but the cylinder went farther in this test.’ Keep both statements.
Suggest one further question after comparing a car on two surfaces.
For example, ‘Would a third surface give a different distance?’ Accept a related investigable question.

AC9S1I06.title: Make your science report useful to someone else
AC9S1I06.goal: Communicate an observation with labels, evidence and suitable vocabulary.
AC9S1I06.model: Improve this report: ‘It went better there.’ The result was a car travelling 9 blocks on a board and 4 on a rug.
steps: Name the object and the two places being compared.
Include the observed results and the measurement unit.
Write: ‘The toy car travelled 9 blocks on the board and 4 blocks on the rug. In this test it travelled farther on the board.’ Add a labelled drawing or table.
AC9S1I06.mistake: Do not write a prediction as if it were a result. Use ‘I predict’ before a test and ‘I observed’ when reporting evidence.
checks: Why is ‘the sponge changed shape when I pushed it’ clearer than ‘it changed’?
Look for the named object, action and change.
It tells the reader what was tested, what was done and what was observed.
Which label helps a drawing of a measured plant: ‘nice’ or ‘height: 6 blocks’? Explain.
Choose information someone can use to understand the result.
‘Height: 6 blocks’ communicates an observation and its unit.
homework: Describe one safe observation using the sentence ‘I observed __ when __.’ Add a labelled drawing.
Accept a clear observed object or change linked to an action or condition, with relevant labels.
Write one sentence comparing the car's two distances in the model above.
For example, ‘The car travelled farther on the board: 9 blocks compared with 4 blocks on the rug.’
